mmaths-2019-mathathon-01.title: Exchange argument and a short table
mmaths-2019-mathathon-01.body:
Seven small pizzas ($42$ slices, $28$ dollars) can be replaced by three large pizzas ($42$ slices, $27$ dollars), so an optimal purchase has at most $6$ small pizzas. For $S=0,\dots,6$ small pizzas, the number of large pizzas needed is $L=\lceil\frac{400-6S}{14}\rceil$:

| $S$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $L$ | 29 | 29 | 28 | 28 | 27 | 27 | 26 |
| cost | 261 | 265 | 260 | 264 | 259 | 263 | 258 |

The minimum cost is $258$ dollars with $26$ large and $6$ small pizzas (that is $364+36=400$ slices).

**Answer: 26**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-02.title: Geometric series
mmaths-2019-mathathon-02.body:
Her first tails comes on flip $n$ with probability $2^{-n}$, and then she has had $n-1$ heads. An even number of heads means $n$ is odd: $\frac12+\frac18+\frac1{32}+\cdots=\frac{1/2}{1-1/4}=\frac23$.

**Answer: 2/3**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-02.title: Recursion
mmaths-2019-mathathon-02.body: Let $p$ be the probability of an even number of heads. On the first flip she gets tails (probability $\frac12$, zero heads: even) or heads (probability $\frac12$), after which she needs an odd number of further heads, probability $1-p$. So $p=\frac12+\frac12(1-p)$, giving $p=\frac23$.

mmaths-2019-mathathon-03.title: Cancel factorials
mmaths-2019-mathathon-03.body:
Divide both sides by $(n+1)!$: $n!=(n+2)(n+3)(n+4)$. For $n=6$: $720=8\cdot9\cdot10$. The left side grows faster: for $n<6$ it is smaller (e.g. $n=5$: $120<7\cdot8\cdot9=504$) and for $n>6$ it is larger. So $n=6$.

**Answer: 6**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-04.title: Multisets of mix-ins
mmaths-2019-mathathon-04.body:
The mix-ins form a multiset of size $1$, $2$ or $3$ from $8$ types: $\binom{8}{1}+\binom{9}{2}+\binom{10}{3}=8+36+120=164$ (multisets of size $k$ from $8$ types number $\binom{8+k-1}{k}$). Times $10$ flavors: $1640$.

**Answer: 1640**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-04.title: Direct count
mmaths-2019-mathathon-04.body: Size $1$: $8$. Size $2$: two equal ($8$) or two different ($\binom82=28$): $36$. Size $3$: all equal ($8$), two equal and one different ($8\cdot7=56$), all different ($\binom83=56$): $120$. Total $164$, and $164\cdot10=1640$.

mmaths-2019-mathathon-05.title: Symmetry
mmaths-2019-mathathon-05.body:
The expression is symmetric about $x=-\frac72$. Put $x=t-\frac72$. Then it becomes $\left(t-\frac72\right)^2+\left(t-\frac12\right)^4+\left(t+\frac12\right)^4+\left(t+\frac72\right)^2=2t^2+\frac{49}2+2t^4+3t^2+\frac18=2t^4+5t^2+\frac{197}{8}$, which is minimized at $t=0$ with value $\frac{197}8$.

**Answer: 197/8**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-06.title: Compare candidates and bound
mmaths-2019-mathathon-06.body:
The base area is $\frac{960}{15\pi}=\frac{64}{\pi}=\pi r^2$, so $r=\frac8\pi$ and the circumference is $16$. The shortest surface path between the centers of the two bases goes from the center to the rim ($r$), down the side ($15$) and to the other center ($r$): length $15+2r=15+\frac{16}{\pi}\approx20.09$.

Upper bound for any two points $P,Q$ (distance meaning the shortest surface path): both on the side: $\le\sqrt{8^2+15^2}=17$ (unroll the side; horizontal gap at most half the circumference). One on a base, one on the side: go to the nearest rim point (at most $r$ away) then along the side, at most $r+17<20.09$. Both on the same base: at most $2r$. $P$ on the top base at distance $\rho_P$ from its center and $Q$ on the bottom base at $\rho_Q$: go to the rim point above the rim point nearest to $Q$ or nearest to $P$: the two options have lengths at most $15+(r+\rho_P)+(r-\rho_Q)$ or $15+(r-\rho_P)+(r+\rho_Q)$ (the farthest/nearest rim point is $r\pm\rho$ away), and the smaller of the two is at most $15+2r$. So the maximum is $15+\frac{16}{\pi}$.

**Answer: $15+\frac{16}\pi$**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-07.title: Change variables
mmaths-2019-mathathon-07.body:
Put $u=x+y$, $v=x-y$ (a bijection of the plane, so it preserves the number of solutions). Then $x^2+y^2=\frac{u^2+v^2}{2}=8$ gives $u^2+v^2=16$, and the second equation is $u=v^2+a$. Substituting $v^2=u-a$: $u^2+u-a-16=0$. Each root $u$ with $u>a$ gives two values $v=\pm\sqrt{u-a}$, a root $u=a$ gives one value, and $u<a$ none. To get exactly $3$ solutions we need one root $u=a$ and another root $>a$. $u=a$ is a root iff $a^2=16$. The other root is $-1-a$: for $a=4$ it is $-5<4$ (only $1$ solution), for $a=-4$ it is $3>-4$ (then $1+2=3$ solutions).

**Answer: -4**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-08.title: Factor and count powers of 2
mmaths-2019-mathathon-08.body:
$n^4-13n^2+36=(n^2-4)(n^2-9)=(n-2)(n+2)(n-3)(n+3)$.

*$n$ even:* $n-3,n+3$ are odd. Write $n=4m'+2$ (if $n\equiv0\pmod 4$ then $n\pm2\equiv2\pmod4$ and the product $(n-2)(n+2)$ has only $2^2$). Then $(n-2)(n+2)=4m'\cdot(4m'+4)=16\,m'(m'+1)$, whose power of $2$ is $2^{4}$ times the power of $2$ in $m'$ or $m'+1$ (one of them is odd). With $n\le1000$ we have $m'\le249$, and the largest power of $2$ dividing $m'$ or $m'+1$ is $128$ (for $m'=127$ or $128$). So the largest power is $2^4\cdot2^7=2^{11}$.

*$n$ odd:* $n-2,n+2$ are odd and $(n-3)(n+3)=4p(p+3)$ with $n=2p+3$, $p\le498$; $p$ and $p+3$ have opposite parity, so the power of $2$ is $4$ times that of the even one, at most $4\cdot256=2^{10}$.

So the maximum is $2^{11}=2048$, attained e.g. at $n=514$ ($n-2=512$, $n+2=516=4\cdot129$).

**Answer: 2048**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-09.title: Check small n, then a counterexample
mmaths-2019-mathathon-09.body:
A ray from $p$ through $q$ coincides with the ray through $r$ exactly when $q,r$ lie on the same side of $p$ on a line through $p$. Call $p$ *good* if this never happens.

$n=2$: vacuous (two points are always collinear). $n=3$: three non-collinear points; every point is good. $n=4$: if no three are collinear, any point is good; otherwise three points $A,B,C$ lie on a line and the fourth point $D$ is off it, and $D$ is good (it sees $A,B,C$ on three different rays since $D\notin\ell$).

$n=5$: if no three points are collinear, any point is good. If four lie on a line $\ell$, the fifth point (off $\ell$) is good. Otherwise some line has exactly three points $A,B,C$ (in this order) and the other two points $D,E$ are off the line. The middle point $B$ sees $A$ and $C$ on opposite rays; it fails only if $B,D,E$ are collinear with $D,E$ on the same side of $B$, say $D$ between $B$ and $E$. Then $D$ is good: it sees $B$ and $E$ on opposite rays, and the rays to $A,B,C,E$ are pairwise different because $D,A,B$ ($D,B,C$; $D,A,C$; $D,A,E$ would force $D\in\ell$ or $A=B$ etc.) are never collinear. So the statement holds for $n=5$.

$n\ge6$: put $n-2$ points $L_1,\dots,L_{n-2}$ on a line $\ell$ and two points $Q,R$ off $\ell$ with $L_1$ the midpoint of $QR$. Each $L_i$ has at least two other points of $\ell$ on one side (as $n-2\ge4$), $Q$ sees $L_1$ and $R$ on the same ray, and so does $R$. No point is good, so the statement is false.

The sum of the $n$ for which it is true is $2+3+4+5=14$.

**Answer: 14**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-10.title: The 1s must move
mmaths-2019-mathathon-10.body:
The digits $12121213131415$ are, in positions $1,\dots,14$: $1$ in the seven odd positions, and $2,2,2,3,3,4,5$ in the seven even positions. In the new number no digit may stay in its old place, so no $1$ can be in an odd position. Hence the seven $1$s fill exactly the seven even positions, and the digits $2,2,2,3,3,4,5$ fill the odd positions (where they automatically differ from the old digit $1$). The number of ways is $\frac{7!}{3!\,2!}=420$.

**Answer: 420**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-11.title: Cross-multiply
mmaths-2019-mathathon-11.body:
$ rac{a+3}{b+4}= rac ab+ rac34= rac{4a+3b}{4b}$ gives $4b(a+3)=(b+4)(4a+3b)$, i.e. $4ab+12b=4ab+3b^2+16a+12b$, so $3b^2+16a=0$ and $a=- rac{3b^2}{16}$. So $a$ is a nonpositive integer with $16\mid3b^2$, i.e. $4\mid b$. Writing $b=4k$ ($k
e0$ since $b
e0$) gives $a=-3k^2$, whose largest value is $-3$ at $k=\pm1$ ($b=\pm4$; $b=-4$ is excluded because $b+4
e0$, but $b=4$ works).

**Answer: -3**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-12.title: Longitude bookkeeping
mmaths-2019-mathathon-12.body:
Moving $5\pi$ inches north puts him at latitude $\phi=\frac{5\pi}{r}$ (in radians). The latitude circle there has radius $r\cos\phi$, so moving $\pi$ inches east changes his longitude by $\frac{\pi}{r\cos\phi}$. Moving $5\pi$ south returns him to the equator, and moving $2\pi$ inches west changes the longitude by $-\frac{2\pi}{r}$. He ends where he started iff the net change is a multiple of $2\pi$:
$$\frac{\pi}{r\cos\phi}-\frac{2\pi}{r}=2\pi m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{1}{\cos\phi}-2=2mr\qquad(m\in\mathbb Z).$$
If $r>15$ then $\phi<\frac\pi3$, so $1<\frac1{\cos\phi}<2$ and the left side lies in $(-1,0)$; but $2mr$ is $0$ or has absolute value at least $2r>30$. No solution. For $r=15$: $\phi=\frac\pi3$, $\frac1{\cos\phi}=2$, and $m=0$ works ($\pi$ inches east along the latitude circle of circumference $15\pi$ is $\frac1{15}$ of a turn, and $2\pi$ inches west along the equator of circumference $30\pi$ is also $\frac1{15}$ of a turn, so they cancel). So the largest $r$ is $15$.

**Answer: 15**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-13.title: Reflect and find an equilateral triangle
mmaths-2019-mathathon-13.body:
Reflect $X$ in the axis of symmetry of the isosceles triangle (the bisector of $\angle B$) to get $Y$; then $\angle YBC=17^\circ$, $\angle YCB=13^\circ$, $BY=BX$. Since $\angle XBY=94^\circ-2\cdot17^\circ=60^\circ$, triangle $XBY$ is equilateral. Also $\angle BYC=180^\circ-17^\circ-13^\circ=150^\circ$, so $\angle XYC=360^\circ-60^\circ-150^\circ=150^\circ$. Triangles $XYC$ and $BYC$ share $YC$, have $XY=BY$ and equal included angles $150^\circ$: they are congruent, so $CX=CB$. Then in isosceles triangle $CBX$, $\angle CXB=\angle CBX=94^\circ-17^\circ=77^\circ$.

**Answer: 77**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-14.title: Sum formulas
mmaths-2019-mathathon-14.body:
With $N=2019=3\cdot673$: $\sum1=N\equiv0$; $\sum2n=N(N+1)\equiv0$; $\sum8n^3=8\cdot\frac{N^2(N+1)^2}{4}=2N^2(N+1)^2\equiv0$; and $\sum4n^2=\frac{4N(N+1)(2N+1)}{6}=\frac{2N}{3}(N+1)(2N+1)=1346\cdot2020\cdot4039$ (using $\frac N3=673$). Modulo $2019$: $2020\equiv1$ and $4039=2\cdot2019+1\equiv1$, so this term is $\equiv1346$. Hence the remainder is $1346$.

**Answer: 1346**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-15.title: Count linear extensions
mmaths-2019-mathathon-15.body:
The variable $j$ is unconstrained: choose its value in $10$ ways, and then the other nine values are assigned according to their relative order. Among $a,\dots,i$: $a$ and $f$ are below everything else (they are below $b,g$ and hence above... precisely both are smaller than all of $b,c,d,e,g,h,i$): $2$ orders for $\{a,f\}$. Next, $b$ and $g$ are the two smallest of the rest: $2$ orders. Next $c$ and $h$ are the two smallest of what remains: $2$ orders. Finally $d,e,i$ remain with $d<e$ only: $i$ can be before $d$, between $d$ and $e$, or after $e$: $3$ orders. Total $10\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot3=240$.

**Answer: 240**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-16.title: Idempotents modulo 1320
mmaths-2019-mathathon-16.body:
$n$ is equi-powerful iff $1320\mid n(n-1)$. Since $\gcd(n,n-1)=1$, each prime power $8,3,5,11$ in $1320=2^3\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11$ must divide $n$ or $n-1$: $n\equiv0$ or $1$ modulo each of them. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem each of the $2^4=16$ choices gives exactly one residue class mod $1320$, hence one integer in $[1,1320]$.

**Answer: 16**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-17.title: Greedy combinatorial number system
mmaths-2019-mathathon-17.body:
Choose the terms greedily from the top: the largest $n_{10}$ with $\binom{n_{10}}{10}\le2019$ is $14$ ($\binom{14}{10}=1001$; $\binom{15}{10}=3003$ is too big). Remainder $1018$. Then $n_9=13$ ($\binom{13}9=715$), remainder $303$. $n_8=11$ ($\binom{11}8=165$), remainder $138$. $n_7=10$ ($\binom{10}7=120$), remainder $18$. $n_6=7$ ($\binom76=7$), remainder $11$. $n_5=6$ ($\binom65=6$), remainder $5$. $n_4=5$ ($\binom54=5$), remainder $0$. So $j=4$ and the sum is $5+6+7+10+11+13+14=66$.

**Answer: 66**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-18.title: Compare divisor counts
mmaths-2019-mathathon-18.body:
Write $n=2^a3^b13^c\,m$ with $\gcd(m,78)=1$. Then $\tau(26n)=(a+2)(b+1)(c+2)\tau(m)$ and $\tau(6n)=(a+2)(b+2)(c+1)\tau(m)$. So $\tau(26n)>\tau(6n)$ iff $(b+1)(c+2)>(b+2)(c+1)$, i.e. $b>c$.

Count $n\le390$ with $b>c$: if $13\nmid n$ ($c=0$) we need $3\mid n$: there are $130$ multiples of $3$, of which $10$ are multiples of $39$, leaving $120$. If $13\mid n$ then $c\ge1$ and we need $b\ge2$, i.e. $117\mid n$ ($n=117,234,351$, each with $c=1<b$): $3$ values. Total $123$, probability $\frac{123}{390}=\frac{41}{130}$.

**Answer: 41/130**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-19.title: Construction and bound
mmaths-2019-mathathon-19.body:
*Example for $n=7$:* $S=\{35,60,84,420,840,1260,1680\}$: for each $k=2,\dots,7$ exactly six of the seven numbers are divisible by $k$ (e.g. $35$ is the only odd one, only $60$ is not divisible by $7$, etc.).

*Bound:* suppose $n\ge8$. Since $2$ divides exactly $n-1$ elements, exactly one element $s_1$ is odd; as $s_1$ is odd, it is not divisible by $4,6,8$, and since each of $4,6,8$ divides exactly $n-1$ elements, all the other $n-1$ elements are divisible by $4,6,8$. Each of $3,5,7$ misses exactly one element, so at most $3$ of the other elements are not divisible by all of $3,5,7$. Therefore at least $n-1-3\ge4$ elements are divisible by $\operatorname{lcm}(2,\dots,8)=840$. But only $840$ and $1680$ are multiples of $840$ in $[1,2019]$: contradiction. So $n\le7$.

**Answer: 7**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-20.title: Factorial base
mmaths-2019-mathathon-20.body:
Ignore $0!$ (it equals $1!$). In an optimal representation, $i+1$ copies of $i!$ can be replaced by one $(i+1)!$, so each $i!$ is used at most $i$ times; that is the factorial number system, $n=\sum_{i\ge1}d_ii!$ with $0\le d_i\le i$, and $f(n)=\sum d_i$.

For $0\le n<k!$ the digits are $d_1,\dots,d_{k-1}$ and each $d_i$ takes each of its $i+1$ values equally often, so it has average $\frac i2$. Thus $\sum_{n<k!}f(n)=k!\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac i2=k!\cdot\frac{k(k-1)}{4}$. For $k=6$: $720\cdot\frac{30}{4}=5400$. This counts $n=0,\dots,719$ (with $f(0)=0$); replacing $n=0$ by $n=720=6!$ (so $f(720)=1$) gives $5400+1=5401$.

**Answer: 5401**

mmaths-2019-mathathon-21.title: Regroup using the totient sum
mmaths-2019-mathathon-21.body:
$\frac1{101^n-1}=\frac{101^{-n}}{1-101^{-n}}=\sum_{k\ge1}101^{-kn}$, so the sum is $\sum_{n\ge1}\phi(n)\sum_{k\ge1}101^{-kn}$. Everything is positive, so we may regroup by $m=kn$: $\sum_{m\ge1}101^{-m}\sum_{n\mid m}\phi(n)$. Since $\sum_{n\mid m}\phi(n)=m$, this equals $\sum_{m\ge1}m\,101^{-m}=\frac{1/101}{(1-1/101)^2}=\frac{101}{100^2}=\frac{101}{10000}$.

**Answer: 101/10000**
